1:
Henry accounts for the repetition at the outset. This prophecy opens as the previous one did, because there is need of line upon line both for the conviction of Israel's enemies and the comfort of Israel's friends; and he notes that the enemy is brought from the north as the Chaldeans formerly were, quoting the proverb that every evil comes from the north and observing that long afterwards the Roman empire was overrun by northern nations. The mountains are named twice over on his reading, first as a place of temptation where the measure of the invader's iniquity is filled up and then as the place of execution. Keil and Delitzsch head the passage simply as the general announcement of the destruction, and Clarke calls the terms so lofty and comprehensive that they must denote some very extraordinary interposition of providence on the people's behalf, remarking on the art with which the prophet delays the summoning of the birds until later.

Whom the prophecy is about divides them sharply. Clarke reads the whole historically and identifies every element with the campaign of Antiochus: the archers whose bows are struck down are the Persians in his army, the fire sent on Magog is the destruction of the Syrian troops, those dwelling carelessly in the isles are the auxiliaries who came to him from the shores of the Euxine, and the defeat in the midst of Israel is the total rout of his immense army in that very land, where he had profaned the temple and insulted the worship of God. Gill reads it as still future and identifies the country to be burnt as the Ottoman empire, with the slaughter accomplished either by the sword of the Jews and Christian princes or by judgments from heaven. Ellicott takes it apocalyptically, noting that the judgment falls not only on the army in Israel but on the far-distant country of Gog, that the fire is represented in the Apocalypse as coming down from God out of heaven, and that the mention of the isles, a standing expression for the remoter parts of the earth, is added to show the universality of the judgment. Wesley calls it the notable day of recompences against the last great enemies of the church.

One clause is contested on the text itself. Where the received version leaves but a sixth part of the invader, Ellicott observes that the word occurs nowhere else and that the rendering assumes a derivation from the numeral six; even granting that assumption he thinks the marginal renderings as likely to be right, and he judges the derivation probably wrong altogether, since all the ancient versions give a sense answering to the earlier chapter's language of leading and turning. Keil and Delitzsch keep the sixth part in their text. Gill works on the neighbouring verb instead, denying that the turning back means turning from the land of Israel, since the same sentence brings him there, and taking it rather that God turns him about in his own country and leads him where he pleases, so that providence is greatly concerned in the whole affair.

Of the weapons named, Wesley observes that what is said of the bow is to be understood of every other weapon, the bow being singled out because it was most in use among the northern peoples. Clarke keeps the anatomy exact, that the bow is held in the left hand while the arrow is drawn and discharged by the right. On the closing declaration that it is come and it is done, Gill and Wesley agree that the thing is spoken of as accomplished because the event is as certain as if it were already past, and Henry says the same and compares the voice that declared from the throne that it is done.
9:
Whether the seven years of burning and the seven months of burying can be taken literally is the question that governs the passage. Ellicott says they cannot: the notion that the weapons of one army should furnish a whole nation with fuel for seven years is not to be understood literally, and seems inserted to show the meaning must be looked for beyond the letter. He reinforces it with an arithmetic reductio borrowed from another commentator, that a million men burying two corpses apiece daily through the working days of seven months would amount to three hundred and sixty million bodies. Clarke takes a middle course, calling the seven months figurative but admitting a good deal of literal meaning, since many of the defeated hid themselves after the pursuit and died of wounds and hunger, so were not all found at once. Wesley defends the burning on practical grounds, the need of fire in such a country being much less than in his own. Gill takes it plainly, that during those years they would have no need to fetch wood from the field, having a sufficiency of armour.

Why the weapons should be burnt rather than kept is answered two ways. Wesley raises the difficulty himself, that arms which might have served for their own defence are destroyed, and answers that it was done in testimony that God was their defence and that on him only they relied. Clarke makes the bonfires an expression of joy at the destruction of their enemies, adding that domestic use of them would keep the memory alive. Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence through to the reversal that follows, that they shall spoil those who spoiled them.

The valley where the dead are buried is disputed between a real road and an imagined one. Clarke locates it east of the lake, following the Targum, and explains the name from its being a great thoroughfare by which merchants and traders from Syria and the eastern countries went down into Egypt; Wesley gives the same account, deriving the name from the frequent travel through it out of Egypt and Arabia. Ellicott denies both. The name cannot be derived from the passing of the invaders themselves, as though they were a cloud passing over and gone, since the same word recurs in the following verses in a plainly different sense; it denotes rather some thoroughfare, probably imaginary, which the buried bodies are to block up. Wesley draws the irony out of the burial: the invader came to take possession, and possess he shall, but not as he purposed and hoped, for he will possess his house of darkness in the land he invaded.

On the searchers and the city, Gill has the chief men of Israel selecting persons to be daily employed until the work is ended, and Wesley has them going over the whole land because many wounded fugitives died in thickets into which they had crept. Ellicott draws an inference from the searching itself, that the army is not conceived of as perishing gathered in one place but as scattered over the country. Of the name given to the city, Gill reports that it signifies a multitude and that the Greek version renders it a place of many graves; Ellicott says the same and adds the reason the cleansing mattered so much, that under the law the extremest defilement of all was caused by a dead body or by human bones, from which the land could be purified only by burial. Henry turns the labour into a lesson, that times of great deliverance should be times of reformation, that every man should help to the utmost toward cleansing the land from reproach, and that sin is an enemy every man should strive against.
17:
The summons to the birds is explained from custom and from precedent. Clarke finds an allusion to an eastern practice, that when a sacrifice is made the friends and neighbours of the sacrificer are invited to come and feast upon it. Ellicott notes that the representation of a destroying judgment as a sacrifice occurs in two other prophets, and warns at once that the figure is not to be pushed beyond its purpose. Wesley presses it as far as it will go without breaking: the punishment is called a sacrifice which God offers to his own justice, and it is offered on the mountains where more thousands are slain at once than were ever offered anywhere, so that no sacrifice ever was or will be like it. Gill raises the oddity that the address is made to creatures not then in being, which could not have understood the words if they had been, and answers that when the time comes they will be gathered partly by an instinct in nature and partly by a particular direction of providence.

Ellicott then observes what makes these verses hard to read steadily: there is a curious mingling of the figurative and the literal in them, since the princes whose blood is to be drunk are immediately explained by the naming of sacrificial animals, and those animals are in turn interpreted a few lines later as horses and chariots and mighty men and men of war. Wesley describes the same movement as a device with two parts, God taking on the person of one who makes a feast and invites his guests, so that the first invitation is enigmatical, an invitation in a riddle, while what follows is the key to it. Gill keeps the identification plain, that the flesh of the mighty means the soldiers, men of strength and courage fit for war, with whom that army will abound.

Clarke uses the passage to put down a slander. Asking who it is that shall eat and drink, he answers that it is not the Jews, and reports that Voltaire had said they ate human flesh and were here invited by the prophet to eat the flesh and drink the blood of their enemies, which Clarke calls a most unprincipled falsehood, since it is the fowls and the beasts that God invites. He mentions in passing the Scandinavian custom of drinking an enemy's blood from the skulls of the dead, and observes that the feast promised here is to birds and beasts and will be as grateful and as plenteous to them as a feast of rams and lambs and goats.

On the effect of the judgment among the nations, Gill makes the display of glory the ultimate end of the whole strange event, the divine power and goodness set in so clear a light that the heathen cannot but observe it. Ellicott agrees that these verses state the ultimate effect and that the following ones apply it to the captivity then present, but insists the effect is too far-reaching to be limited to that application. He adds two qualifications of his own. The knowledge promised is evidently practical and is expressly said to remain for ever, so that it can only be reckoned realised, and even then in germ only, in the Christian church; and the understanding granted to the nations is that God's dealings shall no longer be misread, nor Israel's sufferings taken for evidence that he wanted power to protect them, all the world seeing instead the reasonableness and the necessity of his punishing even his own. Gill puts the same point from the other side, that the heathen had thought the captivity owing to the weakness of the God the Jews served and the superior strength of their enemies and their enemies' gods.
25:
The turn to mercy at the close is read by all four as the answer to what has gone before, and they differ on how far it reaches. Clarke states the two lessons together: both Israel and the heathen shall know that it was for iniquity that they were given into their enemies' hands, and God will now redeem them in such a way as to prove that he is a merciful God as well as a just one. Gill sets the promise in his own scheme, that the Jews having long been punished for their sins and brought at last to repentance and to faith in Christ, as he holds they will be in the latter day, this word follows. Ellicott explains why the promise stands where it does: it was needed by exiles in their distress that the prophet, at the close of so far-reaching a prophecy, should set out the first step in the long course of events leading to its fulfilment, because that first step was the one of especial interest and comfort to them.

The bearing of shame is glossed three ways that amount to much the same. Clarke takes it as bearing the punishment due to a course of conduct that was their shame and reproach, and names that conduct as idolatry. Wesley reduces it to reproach for their sins. Gill describes the disgrace concretely, of captives and exiles scattered among the nations under manifest tokens of divine anger, and reports an alternative rendering by which the clause becomes a statement that they shall bear their shame rather than a note of time after which the promise takes effect.

Clarke argues from the incompleteness of the historical return that a greater one must be meant. All who chose had liberty to go back, he observes, but many remained behind; so the promise that none shall be left any more may point to a larger restoration in which not one shall remain, and he takes the following verse to intimate that this belongs to the gospel dispensation. He keeps his historical frame in view even here, noting that the conqueror he has identified throughout the chapter had taken many Jews captive and sold them for slaves. On the outpouring at the very end he corrects the tense, that the past form is to be understood as a promise of what God will do, and describes the Spirit's work as enlightening, quickening, purifying and cleansing their hearts until, being completely changed, they become God's people and a praise in the earth.

Gill ends where Clarke does but by his own road. On their future conversion, he says, the worship of God will always be among them and his presence with them; he will take notice of them continually, they will be under his protection and care, and he will never remove his presence from them again, which he gives in the Targum's language of the Shechinah not departing. Ellicott's last word is the more cautious one, that even the promise of return is only the first step of something whose full effect the exiles could not have measured.
